question: A 62-year-old woman has serum calcium 3.1 mmol/L with an elevated PTH of 110 pg/mL (normal 15–65). Phosphate is low-normal. Which condition most likely explains this combination?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sarcoidosis causes non-PTH-mediated hypercalcaemia — PTH is suppressed by the high calcium level.
Correct. In primary hyperparathyroidism, autonomous PTH secretion drives elevated PTH alongside hypercalcaemia. Phosphate is lowered because PTH promotes renal phosphate wasting.
PTHrP-mediated malignancy causes suppressed PTH (high calcium suppresses the parathyroids). PTH would be undetectable or very low.
Vitamin D toxicity causes non-PTH-mediated hypercalcaemia — PTH is suppressed. There is no autonomous PTH drive.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key rule: if PTH is elevated or inappropriately normal alongside hypercalcaemia, the cause is PTH-mediated. PTH should be suppressed by any other cause of high calcium.
Well done. Elevated PTH in the setting of hypercalcaemia is the hallmark of PTH-mediated causes, principally primary hyperparathyroidism.
